items.title: Ed Soph interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, February 9, 2024
items.q: Ed Thigpen told me that Ray Brown just gave him hell when Ed first joined the trio with Oscar because Ed couldn’t play on top of the beat enough for Ray.

ctx.x: Oh yeah. He and Sam Jones man together, they were great, because they both felt that. You know along the same lines, when Ray Brown was here a number of years ago we went out to eat some barbeque and I said, “I’m going to ask you a really stupid question.” He says, “I’m used to it.” I said, “Okay.” I said, “Who’s the most comfortable drummer you’ve played with?” And I mean this man played with everybody. And without blinking an eye he said, “Buddy Rich.” I said, “Buddy!” And I said, “Why?” He says, “Because we…

singer was all pissed off because Buddy wasn’t reading the chart and evidently wasn’t playing things that the guy wanted, was supposed to play. So Dorsey turned to the singer and said, “Don’t worry, it’ll be fine tonight.” So Ray came back for the show that night and he said that Buddy played things that even he didn’t hear could be played. And you know Rich’s aural (A-U-R) memory is the equivalent of a photographic memory. He could hear something once — Joe LaBarbera, who used to rehearse new charts for the band…

Along those same lines, I’m going to read a quote here from a bass player named Neal Caine, who is a fairly young man, I think he’s from New Orleans, a marvelous player who played here. And he was addressing the issue — I think I asked him about bass solos.
